Reverse Engineering ChatGPT Stories?
A Computer Science Perspective on Benzon’s Story Exper-
iments

Who is William Benzon?
Background
▶ PhD in English at SUNY Buffalo;
worked in the intellectual tradition of
David G. Hays with long-standing
research in cognitive science and
computational semantics.
▶ Joined Hays’ computational linguistics
group in 1974.
▶ Independent researcher: literary
theory, cognitive science, AI.
His framework
▶ Cognitive networks:
concepts as nodes,
relations as edges.
▶ Abstract concepts defined
over patterns in stories.
▶ Developed computational
and cognitive theories of
narrative over several
decades.
Key point
Benzon is adomain expertwith a long-standing background in cognitive
science and computational semantics — not a naive literary critic.

Common abstract question

---PAGE---
3
Goal of this presentation
Main question
What can Benzon’s story experiments tell us about the behaviour of
ChatGPT, viewed from a computer science perspective?
▶ Explain Benzon’s method and main hypothesis.
▶ Translate narrative concepts into CS / ML terminology.
▶ Connect his black-box probing to the Haralick–Ramesh performance
characterisation framework.
▶ Show how our Transformer experiments follow the same systems-level
perspective.
Framing
Benzon and Ramesh arecomplementary— same abstract question,
different domains, different levels of quantitative rigour.
---PAGE---
4
The paper in one sentence
Benzon’s idea
Change one element in a ChatGPT story and observe how the rest changes
— as a probe of the model’slearned behaviour.
Source story Perturbation
(change protagonist/antagonist)
New story
(what changed?)
Example: Princess Aurora→Prince Harry / Henry the Eloquent / William the
Lazy.
In systems terms
A controlled input perturbation is applied to a black-box system. The output is
analysed to characterise the system’sbehaviour under perturbation.
---PAGE---
5
Experimental setup
▶ Start from a ChatGPT story about Princess Aurora.
▶ Ask ChatGPT to retell it with a changed protagonist or antagonist.
▶ Align old and new stories paragraph by paragraph.
▶ Highlight differences — interpreted as signs of narrative coherence.
Domain expertise as the measurement instrument
Benzon uses his background as a literary analyst and cognitive scientist to
interpret what is preserved and what changes —black-box probing
mediated by domain knowledge.
Methodological observation
It is not clearly specified whether all 12 experiments were conducted in one
session or independently — this may influence reproducibility and
interpretation.
---PAGE---
6
Benzon’s story trajectory
Benzon divides stories into five segments — a parse-tree-like decomposition:
Segment Function
Donn´e Initial situation / background
Disturbance Problem or threat appears
Plan / Transit Hero reacts and moves toward solution
Enact Main action against the problem
Celebrate Resolution and social recognition
Connection to formal linguistics
These segments resemble astory grammar— a hierarchical decomposition
into structural primitives. Do they reflect latent behavioural regularities of the
model, or are they imposed by the analyst?
---PAGE---
7
Example: Aurora becomes Harry
Aurora
▶ Kind princess
▶ Singing voice
▶ Calms dragon by singing
▶ Returns as hero
Harry
▶ Kind prince
▶ Sword-fighting skills
▶ Defeats dragon in battle
▶ Returns as hero
What is preserved / what changes
Global trajectory (Disturbance, Celebrate) is preserved. The protagonist’s
defining attribute and conflict resolution change. The perturbation propagates
locally, not uniformly.
---PAGE---
8
Example: Aurora becomes William the Lazy
The tension
William must be a heroandbe lazy — two constraints in conflict.
▶ Aurora charges the dragon and sings.
▶ William stays in his castle, concocts a potion, delegates to knights.
▶ Plan/Transit, Enact, and Celebrate all change substantially.
▶ Disturbance remains unchanged — independent of the protagonist.
Systems interpretation
The epithet “lazy” acts as aparameterised constraintshifting the generation
behaviour. The degree of change appears proportional to the semantic
distance from the original character.
---PAGE---
9
Benzon’s main hypothesis
Nested hierarchy of probability distributions
Benzon conjectures that ChatGPT’s generation may be organised
hierarchically across story, segment, sentence, and token levels.
Whole story trajectory
Story segments
Sentences
Tokens
Signal processing view
▶ A possible latent narrative
organisation guides generation.
▶ Each level may constrain the
behaviour below.
▶ What is preserved under
perturbation is consistent with this
hierarchy.

10
Translation into CS / ML language
Benzon’s term CS / ML / systems interpretation
Story trajectory High-level behavioural regularity of generated sequence
Segment Local discourse state; node in a narrative parse tree
Protagonist / antagonist Named agent / primitive in the story grammar
Transformation Controlled input perturbation
Coherence Consistency of generated continuation under structural
constraints
Probability hierarchy Context-dependent conditional distribution over next
tokens
Reverse engineering Black-box behavioural probing via systematic perturba-
tion
Key distinction
Benzon observes output behaviour only — no access to weights, activations,
or attention heads. Systematic, but black-box.

11
Benzon’s approach: black-box behavioural probing
Story +
substitution prompt
ChatGPT
(opaque)
New story
(observed output)
Domain expert interprets
what changed and why
▶ Benzon’s domain expertise is themeasurement instrument.
▶ He identifies which behavioural regularities are preserved and which
change.
▶ Analogous to a vision expert who designs probes based on knowledge of
what features matter.
Key question
Whatbehavioural regularitiesdoes ChatGPT’s training instil — what
learned “recipe” does the model follow?
---PAGE---
12
Haralick & Ramesh: performance characterisation
Core idea
Introducecontrolled perturbationsto a system with known input structure
and measure how output performance degrades as a function of perturbation
parameters.
Component Role
Known input / domain model Ground truth; enables fidelity measurement
Perturbation / operating conditions Controlled input variation
Performance metric Quantitative output characterisation
White/gray/black-box mode Degree of access to system internals
Goal
Move from “it works on my examples” to a rigorousengineering
characterisationof system behaviour and performance limits.
---PAGE---
13
The shared systems-level perspective
Benzon Haralick & Ramesh
System ChatGPT (opaque LLM) Vision algorithm
Known input Assumed / interpreted nar-
rative structure
Synthetic data from known
distribution
Perturbation Character substitution Random noise / operating
conditions
Measurement Domain expert interpretation Statistical metrics
Mode Black-box White / gray / black-box
What is preserved? Story trajectory, coherence Algorithm output under de-
gradation
Common systems perspective
Both ask:what does the system preserve when the input is perturbed?
The difference is the language and level of quantitative rigour.
---PAGE---
14
Mini Replication Study
Motivation
Are Benzon’s observed transformations reproducible? Does session history
affect results?
Characters tested:
▶ William the Lazy
▶ Henry the Eloquent
▶ Prince Harry
Conditions:
▶ Independent sessions
▶ Same-session transformations
Purpose
Preliminary qualitative replication before committing to a full quantitative
protocol — consistent with a black-box probing approach.
---PAGE---
15
Replication Results
Character Main Adaptation Observation
William the Lazy Laziness integrated into actions Consistent
Henry the Eloquent Eloquence changes abilities and arti-
facts
Larger modifications
Prince Harry Title and gender adaptation Close to original
Qualitative observation
Across our small sample, larger semantic differences tended to produce larger
narrative adaptations — consistent with Benzon’s conjecture and the
perturbation–performance relationship in Haralick & Ramesh.
Limitation
Preliminary qualitative replication — not statistical validation.
---PAGE---
16
Segment-Level Analysis
Segment Stability Observation
Donn´e Low Character traits adapted
Disturbance High Conflict episode preserved
Plan / Action Medium Trait-dependent modifications
Celebrate Medium Moral lesson adapted
Systems interpretation
The perturbation isabsorbed differently at each level of the hierarchy.
The Disturbance segment behaves like a stable part of the global trajectory;
Donn´e and Enact are more sensitive — consistent with a hierarchically
organised generative behaviour.
---PAGE---
17
Related paper: 20 versions of a prototypical story
▶ Minimal prompt:story— no structure specified.
▶ 10 stories in one session; 10 in separate sessions.
▶ 19 out of 20 follow the same exploration-and-return archetype.
▶ Session history affects protagonist variety.
What this reveals
Repeated sampling under minimal conditions reveals the model’spreferred
operating behaviour— a learned narrative prior that emerges consistently
without any structural prompt.
Methodological implication
Session context is an uncontrolled variable — a nuisance variable in
Haralick–Ramesh terms that should be controlled in a formal protocol.
---PAGE---
18
Connection to our research project
Inspired by the performance characterisation methodology of Haralick &
Ramesh
Rather than analysing natural stories directly, we construct synthetic
stochastic processes with known statistical properties and measure what the
Transformer preserves.
Benzon Our project
Object Stories Binary Markov sequences
Known structure Assumed narrative structure Transition probabilities
Perturbation Character substitution Bit-flip noise / order / scale
Measurement Domain expert interpretation KLD, MAE, statistical tests
Ground truth Unknown Known stochastic process
Mode Black-box Gray-box / controlled synthetic
---PAGE---
19
Our noise experiment as a quantitative analogue
Setup
Transformers trained on clean Markov sequences; bit-flip noise added only at
test time.
Clean Markov
sequence
Bit-flip noise
(controlled)
Transformer
or k-gram
Generated
sequence
▶ k-gram: error increases with noise — sensitive to input.
▶ Transformer: error stays flat — behaviour dominated by learned weights.
What is preserved?
The Transformer preserves the training distribution even under corrupted
input — generation from learned behaviour, not noisy context.
---PAGE---
20
Connecting back to Benzon
Benzon Our project
Perturbation Change protagonist Add bit-flip noise
What is preserved Story trajectory, global coher-
ence
Transition probabilities
What changes Segment-level attributes Little observed change under
tested noise levels
Interpretation Possible latent narrative or-
ganisation
Distribution approximated in
learned behaviour
Shared finding
Both are consistent with the same phenomenon: model output behaviour is
dominated bylearned organisation, not by the specific input perturbation.
Common systems perspective
Although the domains differ — stories versus stochastic sequences — all
three works investigate the same scientific question: how can we characterise
the behaviour of a complex system by systematically perturbing its inputs and
analysing the outputs?
---PAGE---
21
How could Benzon’s approach be made more rigorous?
Following the Haralick–Ramesh performance characterisation protocol:
▶ Generatenstories per condition — not one example.
▶ Control model version, temperature, top-p, and session history.
▶ Definemperturbation types: gender, role, personality trait, antagonist.
▶ Automatically detect story segments.
▶ Use embeddings to quantify protagonist distance.
▶ Test statistically whether perturbation magnitude predicts segment-level
change.
From observation to characterisation
Move from “I observe a pattern” to “the generated distribution differs
significantly from the reference under a defined metric.”
---PAGE---
22
Conclusion
Takeaway
Benzon and Ramesh share a common systems perspective: perturb, observe
what is preserved, characterise behaviour. Different domains, different rigour
— complementary approaches.
▶ Benzon is a domain expert whose black-box probing is principled and
valuable.
▶ His experimentssuggestthat ChatGPT may preserve narrative structure
under perturbation.
▶ Our noise experiments are consistent with the same phenomenon
quantitatively.
▶ The bridge istransdisciplinary harmonisation— translating narrative
hypotheses into statistically testable claims using the language of
distributions and systems theory.
